chapter_title: Deep Dive into AWS CodeCommit for Advanced Source Control
chapter_summary:
Welcome to the foundational layer of our advanced CI/CD journey: source control with AWS CodeCommit. While you might be familiar with basic Git operations, the DevOps Professional exam demands a deeper understanding of how to leverage CodeCommit's advanced features to build secure, scalable, and efficient source control management (SCM) systems. CodeCommit is a fully managed source control service that hosts secure Git-based repositories, seamlessly integrating with other AWS services. Its primary advantage in an AWS ecosystem is its native integration with IAM for authentication and authorization, eliminating the need to manage separate user directories or SSH keys for your Git users.

Securing your repositories is paramount. Beyond simply creating a repository, you must define who can access it and what actions they can perform. This is achieved through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Instead of relying on generic `AWSCodeCommitPowerUser` policies, we'll delve into crafting fine-grained IAM policies that adhere to the principle of least privilege. For instance, you might grant developers `codecommit:GitPull` and `codecommit:GitPush` permissions on specific repository paths, while granting `codecommit:CreatePullRequest` and `codecommit:MergePullRequest` to team leads. Access to CodeCommit repositories is typically managed using HTTPS Git credentials or SSH keys generated within IAM, which are then configured in the user's local Git client. It's crucial to educate your team on the secure handling of these credentials and to enforce regular rotation policies. A common mistake is to embed IAM user access keys directly into scripts or application code, which is a severe security vulnerability. Always use IAM roles for EC2 instances or CodeBuild projects, and temporary credentials for programmatic access where possible.

Effective branching strategies are critical for team collaboration and managing release cycles. For professional DevOps environments, two popular models are Gitflow and GitHub flow. Gitflow, while more complex, is excellent for projects with strict release cycles, involving `master`, `develop`, `feature`, `release`, and `hotfix` branches. GitHub flow, simpler and more agile, typically revolves around `main` (or `master`) and `feature` branches, with all work flowing through pull requests into `main`. CodeCommit supports all standard Git operations, allowing you to implement any of these strategies. The key is consistency across your team. For example, in a Gitflow model, you might configure CodeCommit to only allow merges into `develop` or `master` via pull requests with specific approval rules, preventing direct pushes to these critical branches.

Pull requests (PRs) are the cornerstone of collaborative code review. In CodeCommit, PRs facilitate discussions, code inspections, and automated checks before changes are merged. Beyond basic PR creation, CodeCommit allows you to define approval rules. These rules can mandate a specific number of approvals from designated IAM users or roles, or even require approval from a specific "approver pool" (e.g., a security team or senior architects). For instance, a rule might state that any change to the `master` branch requires two approvals from members of the `DevOpsAdmins` IAM group. This adds a critical layer of quality control and security. Merge strategies are also important: CodeCommit supports `fast-forward merge`, `squash merge`, and `three-way merge` (the default). Understanding when to use each—e.g., `squash merge` for cleaner history of feature branches, `fast-forward` for simple linear merges—is vital for maintaining a clean and understandable repository history.

Integration with other AWS services is where CodeCommit truly shines in a DevOps context. You can configure Amazon EventBridge (formerly CloudWatch Events) to trigger AWS Lambda functions or Amazon SNS topics based on CodeCommit events, such as pushes to a specific branch, pull request state changes, or comment additions. For example, a Lambda function could automatically start a CodeBuild project whenever code is pushed to the `develop` branch, or an SNS notification could alert a team channel when a pull request is awaiting approval. This event-driven architecture is fundamental to building automated CI/CD pipelines. Furthermore, CodeCommit can be directly used as a source stage in AWS CodePipeline, seamlessly feeding your code changes into your build, test, and deployment processes. When working with large repositories or many small files, consider using Git LFS (Large File Storage) if your project includes large binary assets, though CodeCommit's native support for LFS is limited; you might need to manage LFS objects externally or use alternative storage solutions like S3 for very large files referenced in your code. Always remember to monitor your CodeCommit usage, especially storage, as costs can accrue with large repositories and extensive history.

screens.title: Deep Dive into AWS CodeCommit
screens.subtitle: Advanced source control, secure workflows, and CI/CD integrations

narration.text: Welcome. In this chapter you'll learn how CodeCommit becomes the secure Git backbone for advanced AWS CI/CD workflows. I will show you how native IAM integration removes the need for separate user directories, how to apply least-privilege policies for repository and branch actions, and how to design approval rules so critical branches accept only reviewed changes. We'll compare branching models used in professional teams, look at merge strategies that keep history clean, and explore event-driven integrations with EventBridge, Lambda, CodeBuild, and CodePipeline that automate builds and notifications. You'll also see practical guidance for dealing with large binary assets and for rewriting history when needed. These skills matter because managing access, reviews, and automation at scale prevents accidental outages and keeps audits clean. As you work through the hands-on activity, you'll practice creating a repository, assigning scoped permissions, pushing a feature branch, and applying an approval rule that enforces two approvers. Keep an eye out for common mistakes like embedding long-lived keys in code — we'll correct those patterns. By the end you'll have clear, actionable practices to operate CodeCommit in production-grade environments.

keyIdea.text: CodeCommit provides AWS-native Git hosting where IAM-based access control, approval rules, and event-driven integrations enable secure, automated source control for professional CI/CD workflows.

narration.text: In this first objectives panel we focus on practical skills you'll use immediately. First, you'll configure and secure CodeCommit repositories using IAM and scoped policies so that each person or role only has the permissions they need. This reduces blast radius and simplifies audits. Second, you'll implement advanced branching patterns like Gitflow and GitHub flow inside CodeCommit, choosing the model that fits your release cadence and enforcing it with repository rules. Third, you'll use pull requests and approval rules to require reviews from named users or an approver pool, ensuring code quality and compliance before merges. Fourth, you'll set up notifications and wire CodeCommit events to EventBridge, Lambda, SNS, or CodeBuild so that pushes and pull request state changes automatically start builds or alert teams. Each objective ties to real operations: creating scoped IAM policies, creating branches and pull requests, and configuring EventBridge targets. Practicing these will make your repositories secure, auditable, and integrated into automated pipelines. Every objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify the skill in a live environment.

screens.title: What is AWS CodeCommit?
screens.subtitle: Definition, native IAM integration, and why it matters in AWS CI/CD

narration.text: AWS CodeCommit is a fully managed Git-based source control service hosted by AWS that stores your repositories securely and integrates with AWS identity and automation. Practically, that means you manage access with IAM users, groups, or roles instead of separate account systems, and you can trigger AWS services from repository events. For example, a push to a develop branch can start a CodeBuild job or send a notification through EventBridge to an SNS topic. The key practical benefit is reducing operational overhead: you don't run Git servers, and access control ties into existing AWS policies and audit logs. A common misconception is to treat CodeCommit as merely another Git host; in reality its strength is the tight coupling to IAM and to event-driven automation in AWS. To make this concrete, imagine a team that must ensure only approved code reaches master. With CodeCommit you can require approval rules and enforce merge actions via IAM so direct pushes are disallowed. Takeaway: CodeCommit is not just storage — it is an identity-aware service that becomes the entry point for automated, auditable CI/CD pipelines. How would you design your initial repository permissions to limit risk while enabling developer productivity?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: CodeCommit is managed Git storage with native IAM authentication and event hooks that integrate directly into AWS CI/CD services.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What is AWS CodeCommit?
Core definition
A fully managed, secure Git-based repository service integrated with AWS identity and event systems.
Key properties:
  • Native IAM authentication and authorization for Git operations.
  • Event integration with EventBridge to trigger Lambda, CodeBuild, or notifications.
  • Supports standard Git workflows so teams can adopt branching models they prefer.
Concrete example
When developers push to a feature branch, EventBridge can start a test build. If tests pass and approvers sign off, a merge into master triggers a production pipeline.
Key Takeaway

CodeCommit combines managed Git hosting with AWS identity and event-driven automation, making it a service platform for secure, auditable SCM workflows.

Misconception check
Do not assume CodeCommit is only about storage. Its power lies in identity-based access and event hooks that enable secure pipelines and governance.
Why this matters
Using IAM and approval rules reduces accidental production changes and simplifies compliance, which is critical for enterprise-grade delivery.
Check your understanding
Name one reason you would choose CodeCommit over a self-hosted Git server in an AWS-centric environment.

screens.title: Authentication: IAM, HTTPS Git credentials, and SSH keys
screens.subtitle: How developers and CI systems authenticate to CodeCommit securely

narration.text: Authentication to CodeCommit is managed by IAM, and you can authenticate via HTTPS Git credentials or SSH keys that are generated and associated with an IAM user, or by assuming roles for programmatic access. Start by creating IAM users for human developers if needed, generate HTTPS Git credentials in the console, and store them securely in the developer's credential manager. For automated systems like CodeBuild or EC2, use IAM roles so the service assumes permissions without long-lived static keys. A common mistake is embedding IAM user access keys in scripts or repository files — those keys can be leaked and are difficult to rotate. Instead, prefer role-based access with temporary credentials and, when you must use user credentials, enforce rotation and secrets management. Example: configure a CodeBuild project with a service role that has codecommit:GitPull and codecommit:GetBranch permissions on a repository ARN, so builds can clone securely without manual credentials. Misconception to avoid: SSH vs HTTPS is not a security choice alone; the real control is the IAM permissions attached to the identity. Takeaway: choose credential types to match the actor — human developers use managed HTTPS or SSH credentials, machines and pipelines use roles and temporary credentials.

keyIdea.title: Authentication essentials
keyIdea.text: Use IAM identities for humans and roles for machines; avoid long-lived keys and enforce rotation and temporary credentials for programmatic access.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Authentication: IAM, HTTPS Git credentials, and SSH keys
Authentication flow
Match credential type to actor and scope permissions via IAM.
1
Human developers
Use IAM users with HTTPS Git credentials or SSH keys generated for that user. Store and rotate credentials securely.
2
CI/CD systems
Assign an IAM role to the service (CodeBuild, EC2) so it can assume permissions without static keys.
3
Rotation & secrets
Rotate human credentials and store them in secrets managers. Never hard-code access keys in repositories or pipelines.
Supporting cards
Example
A CodeBuild role with scoped codecommit:GitPull permission lets builds clone repos without manual credential handling, simplifying secure automation.
Common mistake
Embedding IAM user keys in scripts. If leaked, rotate immediately and replace with role-based access for services.
Quick checklist
  • Use roles for machines, credentials for humans only when necessary.
  • Enforce rotation and store secrets in a secure manager.
  • Scope policies to repository ARNs and branch refs.
Key Takeaway

Match credential patterns to the actor and prefer temporary, role-based access for automated systems.

screens.title: Fine-grained IAM policies for CodeCommit
screens.subtitle: Applying least privilege to repository and branch operations

narration.text: Fine-grained IAM policies let you express which CodeCommit actions are allowed, on which repositories or branch references, and for which principals. Rather than granting broad, prebuilt roles, craft policies that allow only codecommit:GitPull or codecommit:GitPush on a specific repository ARN, and further restrict pushes to feature branch patterns. For example, developers can be granted GitPush on refs/heads/feature/* while only leads have MergePullRequest or MergePullRequestByFastForward on master or develop. This minimizes risk and ensures that merges to protected branches pass review gates. A common misconception is that policies must be all-or-nothing; in practice you can combine IAM conditions with resource ARNs and allow or deny specific Git operations. Remember to prefer denies when you want to ensure no direct pushes occur to protected branches for a class of users. Concrete example: allow codecommit:CreatePullRequest and codecommit:CommentOnPullRequest for developers, while reserving codecommit:MergePullRequest for the SeniorDevs approver group. Takeaway: designing scoped statements and using role-based approvers enforces workflow rules in the repository itself, reducing the need for human coordination. Fine-grained IAM policies for CodeCommit means grant explicit codecommit actions on repository arns and branch refs, using denies and role separation to enforce branch protection.. In practical terms, applying least privilege to repository and branch operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Least privilege
keyIdea.text: Grant explicit CodeCommit actions on repository ARNs and branch refs, using denies and role separation to enforce branch protection.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Fine-grained IAM policies for CodeCommit
Policy design pattern
Map actions to roles and repository resources to reduce privileges.
Principle: grant the minimum actions required to perform a task, scoped to repository ARNs and branch refs.
Example mapping: Developers: codecommit:GitPull, codecommit:CreatePullRequest; Leads: codecommit:MergePullRequest.
Use denies: explicitly deny codecommit:GitPush to master for developer group to prevent direct pushes.
Scenario
A team enforces Gitflow: only release managers can merge into master. Give feature authors push access to feature branches and PR creation rights, but deny push to master and require approvers for merges.
Policy snippet (illustrative)
State resource ARNs that include the repository name and use conditions for branch refs. Combine Allow and Deny statements to protect critical refs.
Common mistake
Relying solely on an admin role instead of building scoped policies. Broad policies make accidental destructive actions more likely.
Check your understanding
How would you prevent developers from pushing directly to master while still allowing them to create pull requests?

screens.title: Branching Strategies: Gitflow vs GitHub flow
screens.subtitle: When to choose Gitflow or GitHub flow in CodeCommit

narration.text: Branching strategy determines how code changes move from development to production. Gitflow is structured: it uses master, develop, feature, release, and hotfix branches and fits projects with formal release cycles and versioned releases. Its advantages are clear separation of work and predictable release steps, but it can add overhead with many branch types. GitHub flow is simpler: typically a main branch and short-lived feature branches merged through pull requests; it's well suited to continuous deployment where releases are frequent. In CodeCommit, both models work because CodeCommit supports all standard Git operations. The important operational difference is enforcement: with Gitflow you often require strict approval rules and deny direct pushes to master or develop, while with GitHub flow you may favor rapid merges with automated testing gates. A common misconception is that one model is inherently more secure; security depends on how you implement protections — e. g., approval rules, IAM denies, and automated tests — not the branching model alone. Example: for a regulated product with quarterly releases, Gitflow plus approval rules for develop and master is ideal. For a SaaS product deploying multiple times per day, GitHub flow with robust CI and quick rollbacks may be best. Which trade-offs matter most for your team: predictability and separation, or speed and continuous delivery?

keyIdea.title: Choose by trade-off
keyIdea.text: Pick Gitflow for structured release cycles and GitHub flow for rapid continuous deployment; enforce either with approval rules and IAM controls in CodeCommit.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Branching Strategies: Gitflow vs GitHub flow
Gitflow
Structured model with master, develop, feature, release, and hotfix branches for formal release cycles.
Pros: strong separation between ongoing work and releases; clear process for hotfixes.
Cons: added branching overhead and merge coordination.
When to use
Projects with scheduled releases, strict QA cycles, or versioned deliveries.
GitHub flow
Simpler model with a single main branch and short-lived feature branches merged through pull requests.
Pros: lightweight, faster merges, well-suited to continuous deployment.
Cons: requires strong automated testing and rollback strategies to be safe.
When to use
SaaS teams shipping frequent updates with mature automated tests and rapid rollback capability.
Concrete example
For Gitflow, require two approvals on merges into master and restrict direct pushes via IAM denies.
Misconception
No branching model is a substitute for review gates and automated tests — both are required for safe delivery.
Key Takeaway
Choose the model that aligns with your release and testing processes and enforce it with CodeCommit rules and IAM.

screens.title: Enforcing branch protection: approval rules and IAM denies
screens.subtitle: Prevent direct pushes and require approvals for protected branches

narration.text: To protect critical branches like master or develop, use a combination of CodeCommit approval rules and targeted IAM policies that deny direct pushes. Approval rules allow you to define the number of approvers and an approver pool of IAM users and roles; apply a template to the repository so any pull request targeting protected refs requires the specified approvals. Complement approval rules with IAM denies for users or groups that should never push directly to those branches, ensuring technical enforcement even if a PR bypass were attempted. For example, deny codecommit:GitPush to refs/heads/master for the developer group while granting codecommit:MergePullRequest only to a SeniorDevs IAM group. A common trap is relying on UI habit rather than policy — humans may still try to push; an IAM deny makes that impossible. Also ensure your CI roles that perform merges have explicit permissions to merge by role so automation can comply with the workflow. Takeaway: approval rules provide the review gate, and scoped IAM denies provide a technical lock that prevents direct, unreviewed changes. Enforcing branch protection: approval rules and IAM denies means use approval rules for review gates and iam deny statements to technically block direct pushes to protected refs.. In practical terms, prevent direct pushes and require approvals for protected branches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Branch protection
keyIdea.text: Use approval rules for review gates and IAM deny statements to technically block direct pushes to protected refs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Enforcing branch protection
Two-layer protection pattern
Approval rules for governance; IAM denies for technical enforcement.
Approval rules: specify number of approvals and approver pool for PRs targeting refs like master.
IAM denies: explicitly refuse GitPush to protected refs for developer principals to block direct pushes.
Automation: give merging roles explicit merge permissions so CI can complete merges after approvals.
Concrete scenario
Create an approval rule template requiring two approvers from the SeniorDevs group and associate it with the repo so PRs to master block until satisfied.
Quick steps
  1. Create approval rule template with approver ARNs and approval count.
  2. Associate template with repository and target refs.
  3. Add IAM deny statements for direct pushes to protected refs for developer principals.
Common mistake
Only configuring approval rules and forgetting IAM denies, which lets some principals still push if policies are overly permissive.
Key Takeaway

Combine approval rules with IAM denies and dedicated merge roles to create an enforceable branch protection model.

screens.title: Pull Requests, Approval Rules, and Merge Strategies
screens.subtitle: Designing review workflows and choosing merge behavior for repository history

narration.text: Pull requests are the primary mechanism for code review in CodeCommit, enabling threaded discussions, change diffs, and integration checks before merges occur. Approval rules supplement PRs by defining who must approve and how many approvals are required, either by listing IAM users and roles or by referencing an approver pool. Merge strategies determine how the target branch history is updated: fast-forward merges keep linear history when possible, squash merges condense many feature commits into one tidy commit, and three-way merges resolve divergent histories by creating a merge commit. The choice matters: use squash to simplify history for short-lived feature branches, fast-forward when you want a linear timeline, and three-way when histories have diverged and you need to preserve commit context. A misconception is that squash removes accountability — it preserves author metadata but creates a single commit, so include clear commit messages. Concrete example: require two approvals for merges into master and prefer squash merges to keep master history concise. Always ensure your approval rules and IAM permissions align with allowed merge strategies so only the intended principals can merge in the chosen way. Takeaway: combine PRs, approval rules, and merge strategy consistently to balance traceability and repository hygiene.

keyIdea.title: Review & merge
keyIdea.text: Use pull requests with approval rules to enforce reviews, and select a merge strategy that aligns with your team's traceability and history cleanliness goals.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Pull Requests, Approval Rules, and Merge Strategies
Pull request lifecycle
Create PR → reviewers comment and approve → automated checks run → merge when rules satisfied.
Fast-forward
Linear history when target can advance without merge commits.
Squash merge
Combine feature commits into one for a cleaner main history.
Three-way merge
Creates a merge commit to preserve non-linear histories.
Example workflow
Developers push features, create PRs, automated tests run; PRs require two approvers listed in an approval rule before a merge is allowed.
Misconception
Choosing a merge strategy changes history shape but does not replace the need for reviews and automated checks; all three should work together.
Pro tip
Use squash for many small commits and include a condensed changelog in the squash commit message to retain traceability.
Key Takeaway

Define review rules and choose a merge strategy that supports your team's auditability and history needs.

screens.title: Integrating CodeCommit with AWS Automation
screens.subtitle: EventBridge, Lambda, CodeBuild, SNS, and CodePipeline in event-driven workflows

narration.text: CodeCommit events can feed an event-driven automation architecture so repository activity becomes the source of truth for CI/CD pipelines. Use EventBridge rules to capture events like pushes, pull request state changes, or comments, and route them to targets such as Lambda functions, SNS topics, or CodeBuild projects. For example, a push to develop can trigger EventBridge which starts a Lambda that validates repository metadata and then starts a CodeBuild project. Alternatively, use CodeCommit directly as the source stage for CodePipeline to send commits into a multi-stage pipeline. Notifications can be sent to Slack or email via SNS when PRs await approval. A frequent misconception is that CodeCommit must directly call every service — instead, EventBridge centralizes routing and decouples producers and consumers. Concrete example: configure EventBridge to kick off a CodeBuild test job on pushes to refs/heads/develop and send a notification if tests fail. Takeaway: EventBridge is the glue for reliable, auditable automation triggered by CodeCommit events. Integrating CodeCommit with AWS Automation means use eventbridge as the central router for codecommit events and connect to lambda, codebuild, sns, or codepipeline for automated, decoupled ci/cd flows.. In practical terms, eventbridge, lambda, codebuild, sns, and codepipeline in event-driven workflows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event-driven automation
keyIdea.text: Use EventBridge as the central router for CodeCommit events and connect to Lambda, CodeBuild, SNS, or CodePipeline for automated, decoupled CI/CD flows.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Integrating CodeCommit with AWS Automation
Event-driven architecture
Use EventBridge to route repository events to automation targets.
EventBridge
Central event bus capturing commit and PR events.
Lambda
Custom validation, checks, or orchestration logic on events.
CodeBuild / CodePipeline
Run builds and pipelines triggered by repository changes.
Concrete example
Push to develop → EventBridge rule catches the push → starts a CodeBuild test project. On failure, an SNS notification alerts the team.
Misconception
Don't attempt to tightly couple CodeCommit to a single consumer; EventBridge decouples services and simplifies retries and auditing.
Pro tip
Centralize routing logic in EventBridge and perform small, idempotent actions in Lambdas to keep automation resilient.
Key Takeaway

Use EventBridge to connect CodeCommit events to CI/CD and notification targets for reliable, auditable automation.

screens.title: Handling large files and repository hygiene
screens.subtitle: Removing large blobs, Git LFS considerations, and practical prevention strategies

narration.text: Large binary files in a Git repository cause performance issues for cloning and history operations. If a developer accidentally pushes a large binary, the recommended remediation is to rewrite history locally using tools designed for this task, such as BFG Repo-Cleaner or a history rewrite workflow, and then force-push the cleaned history back to CodeCommit. This is a destructive operation and requires coordinating with the team so everyone reclones or rebases onto the new history. Prevention is preferable: do not store large binaries in the repository. Because CodeCommit's native Git LFS support is limited, choose one of two approaches: store large assets in S3 and commit only references to those objects, or manage LFS objects externally in an LFS-capable storage and reference them in your workflow. To prevent future large-file commits, implement pre-push checks on clients or set up a push-validation pipeline triggered by pushes that rejects offending commits and notifies the author. A common misconception is that deleting the file in a later commit removes it from history — it does not. Proper history rewrite is required. Takeaway: combine prevention, monitoring, and careful remediation to maintain repository performance and developer productivity.

keyIdea.title: Repo hygiene
keyIdea.text: Avoid storing large binaries in Git; use S3 or external LFS and rewrite history carefully when large files are accidentally committed.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Handling large files and repository hygiene
Problem & remediation
Large files slow clones and increase storage cost. Rewriting history removes them but requires coordination.
Remediation: use BFG or git filter-branch locally, purge the file from all history, and force-push the cleaned repository. Coordinate team actions and re-clone as needed.
Prevention: store large binaries in S3 or external LFS and commit only references to objects; add client-side checks to reject large files.
Monitoring: watch repository storage and clone times; large size growth indicates needed cleanup or a system change.
Concrete action
If a 500 MB binary lands on master, rewrite history locally to remove it, force-push, and then update every developer to the new history to avoid corruption.
Common mistake
Assuming deleting the file in a later commit reduces repository size; the blob still exists in history until rewritten.
Key Takeaway

Use off-repo storage for large assets and implement checks to prevent large commits; rewrite history only after a coordinated plan.

screens.title: Hands-on: Create a secure repository and approval rule
screens.subtitle: CLI steps and approval rule template — follow along in your terminal

narration.text: In this hands-on walkthrough you'll perform the essential steps: create a CodeCommit repository, configure an IAM user with scoped permissions and HTTPS Git credentials, clone the repo, push a feature branch, and create an approval rule template that requires two approvals. First, create the repository using the CodeCommit create-repository command. Next, create an IAM user with a policy granting only the necessary codecommit actions on the repository and generate HTTPS Git credentials in the IAM console; store these securely. Then clone the repository, make a small change, create a feature branch, commit, and push the branch. Create a JSON approval rule that targets the master branch and specifies two approvers by ARN, create the approval-rule-template using the CLI, and associate it to the repository. A common mistake is testing merges without verifying the approval rule is associated; confirm the rule is active before attempting to merge. When you practice this workflow, ensure you use roles for automation and do not embed credentials in scripts. After completing these steps you will have a repository protected by a review gate and a realistic lab to validate your policies and processes.

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: You will create a repo, scoped IAM credentials, push a feature branch, then create and apply an approval rule template requiring two approvers.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Hands-on: Create a secure repository and approval rule
Terminal demo (read-only)
Commands to run in your terminal. These are shown for study; speak them aloud as actions rather than pasting secrets into files.
aws codecommit create-repository --repository-name my-secure-app --repository-description "Repository for a secure application"

# Clone, commit, push
git clone https://git-codecommit.REGION.amazonaws.com/v1/repos/my-secure-app
cd my-secure-app
echo "Initial commit" > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git push origin master

git checkout -b feature/new-feature
echo "New feature content" >> feature.txt
git add feature.txt
git commit -m "Add new feature"
git push origin feature/new-feature

# Approval rule JSON (update ACCOUNT_ID)
{
  "approvalRuleName": "RequireTwoApprovals",
  "approvalRuleContent": "{\"Version\":\"1.0\",\"DestinationReferences\":[\"refs/heads/master\"],\"Statements\":[{\"Type\":\"Approvers\",\"NumberOfApprovalsNeeded\":2,\"ApprovalPoolMembers\":[\"arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:user/dev-user\",\"arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:role/CodeReviewerRole\"]}]}"
}

aws codecommit create-approval-rule-template --cli-input-json file://approval-rule.json
aws codecommit associate-approval-rule-template-with-repository --approval-rule-template-name RequireTwoApprovals --repository-name my-secure-app
Notes
  • Replace REGION and ACCOUNT_ID with your values. Do not paste credentials into scripts.
  • Generate HTTPS Git credentials in the IAM console for a human user, or assign a role to CodeBuild for CI access.
Common pitfall
Failing to replace sample ARNs or leaving account IDs in templates. Always validate ARNs before creating templates.
Key Takeaway

Practice the repo creation and approval-rule association in a sandbox account, and never use long-lived keys in pipeline code.

screens.title: Assessment scenarios and common mistakes
screens.subtitle: Exam-style questions and how to reason about correct answers

narration.text: This screen lays out assessment-style scenarios and explains the reasoning to choose correct solutions. Scenario one: you must prevent direct pushes to master and require two approvals from a SeniorDevs group. The correct approach combines IAM denies for developer principals on pushes to protected refs with an approval rule template targeted at master requiring two approvers drawn from SeniorDevs. The deny blocks direct pushes technically, and the approval rule enforces the review gate at the PR level. Scenario two: a large binary was pushed and cloning became slow. The correct remediation is to rewrite the repository history locally with a tool like the BFG or git filter-branch to remove the blob, then force-push the cleaned history, and coordinate a team-wide re-clone. Prevent this by using S3 for binaries or implementing checks to reject large files. A common exam trap is recommending simple deletion in a later commit — that does not remove the historical blob. When answering scenario questions, identify the constraint, map it to CodeCommit features like approval rules or EventBridge, and state the operational steps including coordination and rollback plans. Takeaway: practice mapping requirements to the two complementary controls: IAM policies and CodeCommit approval rules, and plan for operational coordination when rewriting history.

keyIdea.title: Assessment logic
keyIdea.text: Combine IAM denies and approval rules for protection, and use history rewrite plus prevention strategies for large-file remediation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Assessment scenarios and common mistakes
Assessment scenarios
Work through the scenario logic and identify the correct CodeCommit and IAM features to use.
Q1: Enforce two approvals and block direct pushes to master
Answer: Create an approval rule template requiring two approvers from SeniorDevs and associate it with the repo. Add IAM deny statements for developers to block direct pushes to refs/heads/master while granting merge permissions to the approver role.
Q2: Large binary pushed to master
Answer: Rewrite history locally with a history-clean tool and force-push the cleaned history, then implement prevention via S3 or pre-push checks. Deleting in a later commit is not sufficient.
Exam strategy
Always map the requirement to CodeCommit features and IAM controls, then describe operational steps including coordination, role updates, and testing. Watch for distractors that suggest only UI changes or optimistic deletion of files.
Key Takeaway

Answer exam questions by specifying both policy enforcement and operational steps; combine IAM, approval rules, and coordinated remediation when needed.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Compact reference of essential terms and ideas

narration.text: Let's reinforce the most important concepts from this chapter. First, CodeCommit is a managed Git service that integrates with IAM, enabling identity-aware access control and event routing. Second, use fine-grained IAM policies to apply the principle of least privilege by granting specific CodeCommit actions on repository ARNs and branch refs. Third, pull requests and approval rules form the cornerstone of code review, and merge strategies like fast-forward, squash, and three-way affect your history and traceability. These three concepts — managed hosting with IAM, least-privilege policies, and review/merge mechanics — are the practical building blocks you'll use when designing secure, automated source control in AWS. Keep them in mind as mental checks whenever you configure repositories or design pipelines. screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three final flashcards to carry forward

narration.text: These final flashcards reinforce practical rules you can act on immediately. First, always prefer IAM roles and temporary credentials for automated systems and rotate any human Git credentials. Second, combine approval rules with IAM denies to protect critical branches and ensure merges pass approval checks. Third, avoid storing large binaries in your Git history; use S3 or an external LFS and implement history-cleaning and detection policies when problems occur. Keep these three practices as quick checks when you design or audit a CodeCommit repository.
